stories.title_en: The Usefulness of Useless Knowledge [pdf] (1939)

comments.author: gopher_space
comments.text:
Classic article, and the software industry is familiar with microcosms of the thesis e.g. justifying a R&D budget or defending dev "lifestyle".  We're also familiar with both sides of the situation via STEM elitism.
It feels like there's an essential tension between two ways to view a statement like "unknowable value", and our alignment depends on our interest in the subject.     The source of tension is resource allocation, and the timelessness of this thesis revolves around long-term planning and control issues.

comments.author: alexpotato
comments.text:
A couple points:
1. Random knowledge can often be used to build a "map" to conclusions that turn out to be useful
e.g. someone once asked me what what country was number 2 in terms of total airplane flights (the US is number 1).
I deduced:
- had to be a big country
- with spread out cities
- and required flying instead of driving
I remembered reading that Brazil has traffic that is so bad and such poor security that people commute to work via helicopter. Even though I wasn't sure it was Brazil, I could guesstimate that it was indeed Brazil.
2. Random facts are great for creating shared references or metaphors across cultural or organizational boundaries.
e.g. I worked with many people from India over the years and being able to quote a famous Bollywood movie or Indian mythology was excellent at helping build rapport etc
3. I was watching a documentary on an Army jungle survival school. The instructor mentioned:
"People ask me if they should read survival guides or biographies of people who survived a calamity. I 100% say yes b/c the after action reports of people surviving are filled with stories of 'then I remembered this random fact from years ago that helped me survive'."

comments.author: incognito124
comments.text: I frequently go to pub quizzes, and there'a this shared opinion that its mostly useless trivia there. But the underappreciated fact I think most miss is that pub quiz trivia sets you up well for understanding wider historical context. Knowing random facts about countries and capitals and some of the better known events or works of art is not just a party trick, it can help you explain other future events. It's like a web of facts that go together

comments.author: vunderba

I often compare trivia and even factoids to a well-stocked larder. The more ingredients you have, the more potential recipes you can devise.
Ken Jennings also made a great point in one of his books: one of the most undervalued things about trivia and knowing
"a little about a lot"
is that it enables you to engage with people about their hobbies and interests at a more meaningful level.
For example, if somebody tells me that they enjoy juggling, asking if they've mastered mills mess or the box pattern is likely to engender far more engaging conversation than the rather pedestrian

comments.author: hazrmard
comments.text:
Perplexity is not defined in the article. FYI:
Perplexity is the degree of surprise the model has in predicting the next token, over a sequence of tokens. At the worst case, perplexity is equal to the size of the vocabulary. At the best case, perplexity is 1.
So, given a sequence of tokens, "e = m c ^ 2", if the p(token | prev tokens) = 1 for every token, perplexity ends up being 1. If, however, it's a random predictor, the p(token | prev tokens) is 1/vocab for every token, and perplexity ends up being len(vocab).
The article plots log(perplexity) on the y-axis, which puts the best case at 0 (i.e. log 1).

I argued this point in a 2008 paper:
https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-69134-1_...
I elaborated on this idea in my 2011 book:
https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.5466
I used the word "reusability" to express the idea that the world models obtained via the large scale data compression task could be repurposed for other tasks.

Attempts at governance are futile until we recognize that we have built a machine and set it on its course. Instead, we pretend that the market is a natural phenomenon best left alone, and we fail to hold its mechanism designers to account. We need to tear down and rebuild that machine, reprogramming it so that human flourishing, not corporate profit, becomes its goal.
This article has useful insights. It points out that capitalism is an optimization engine for something. Shareholder value and CEO compensation, mostly. It reminds us of something that many people would prefer be forgotten - capitalism operates under rules set by governments, and those shape the market. Tax law matters - what's deductible warps spending patterns. Bankruptcy law matters - who gets left holding the bag? Corporation law matters - how immune are executives from the consequences of their decisions? Labor law matters - do people go to jail for wage and hour law violations?
All of those are changeable by legislation. Most have become much more favorable to companies since 1970. That's not necessarily permanent. We had a New Deal in the 1930s, following the Gilded Age of the 1920s and the crash of 1929.

comments.text:
For the price and complexity of building a good Linux-based time server I'd heavily recommend looking at FPGA-based solutions instead. x86 platforms also have PCIe PTM and TGPIO options available[0], which are tad better than the common ARM equivalents and GPIO interrupts.
In general Pi-s are relatively bad for timekeeping. Not just the NIC (which can be replaced by hats with their own), there are also oscillator replacement mods[2] to work around this to some extent. Though all this still leaves many other sources of timekeeping error.
So if the goal is low-cost precise timekeeping, one can assemble something FPGA-based[2] for quite a bit less money, that can reach very low noise figures. You can spend the remaining money on the GNSS antenna and receiver instead.
I'm also sure a FPGA-based approach could be taken even further with some external timekeeping chips available and the FPGA could just do the NTP/PTP protocol stuff.
